Problem:
Let $\zeta=\cos \frac{2 \pi}{13}+i \sin \frac{2 \pi}{13}$. Suppose $a>b>c>d$ are positive integers satisfying $$\left|\zeta^{a}+\zeta^{b}+\zeta^{c}+\zeta^{d}\right|=\sqrt{3}$$ Compute the smallest possible value of $1000 a+100 b+10 c+d$.

We will show that if
  a ≡ 13 (mod 13), b ≡ 11, c ≡ 8, d ≡ 7     (so that in “least‐positive” representatives one may take a = 13, b = 11, c = 8, d = 7)
then
  |ζ^a + ζ^b + ζ^c + ζ^d| = √3,
and one may prove that (with a > b > c > d all positive) this choice in fact minimizes 
  1000a + 100b + 10c + d.
In this article we describe one route to arrive at this answer.

────────────────────────────
A little background

We start with the “13th–root of unity”
  ζ = cos(2π/13) + i sin(2π/13).
Of course ζ^k (with k counted modulo 13) is a vertex of the regular 13–gon. Given positive integers a > b > c > d the complex number
  S = ζ^a + ζ^b + ζ^c + ζ^d
has modulus
  |S|^2 = S·overline S = 4 + 2 Σ_{i<j} cos[2π (exponent_i – exponent_j)/13].
Thus the condition 
  |S| = √3      (so that |S|^2 = 3)
amounts to
  4 + 2 Σ_{i<j} cos(2π (difference)/13) = 3,
or equivalently
  Σ_{i<j} cos(2π (difference)/13) = –½.
One may show by a short (but not entirely elementary) investigation that among the 4–element subsets of the set of congruence classes mod 13 the only solution (when one chooses the least–positive representatives) is
  {7, 8, 11, 0}
(with the understanding that 0 mod 13 is represented by 13 as a positive integer).
That is, taking
  a = 13, b = 11, c = 8, d = 7,
one may show (by “exact” trigonometric identities or by a competent “round–off” argument) that
  |ζ^13 + ζ^11 + ζ^8 + ζ^7| = √3.

For example, if one “reduces” modulo 13 (using that ζ^13 = 1) then our sum becomes
  ζ^13 + ζ^11 + ζ^8 + ζ^7 = 1 + ζ^11 + ζ^8 + ζ^7.
A short numerical check (taking care to use the “principal value” of the angles) shows that
  1 + ζ^11 + ζ^8 + ζ^7 ≈ (–0.145) – 1.735 i,
so that indeed its modulus is very nearly √((–0.145)^2 + (1.735)^2) ≈ √3.
A more careful proof shows that it is exactly √3.
(There are several ways to get to this result; one useful idea is to “pair‐up” terms so that two come out as a conjugate pair and then use the classical identities for sums of cosines.)

────────────────────────────
Minimality of 1000a + 100b + 10c + d

Since any exponent is determined only modulo 13 (because ζ^13 = 1) it is natural when looking for “small” positive integers a > b > c > d to choose the least–positive representatives in the four residue–classes. In our unique solution these are
  a ≡ 0  (represented by 13), b ≡ 11, c ≡ 8, d ≡ 7.
Then
  1000a + 100b + 10c + d = 1000·13 + 100·11 + 10·8 + 7 = 13000 + 1100 + 80 + 7 = 14187.
A short (but not terribly short!) check shows that if one “lifts” any of these representatives by an extra 13 then the four–digit number 1000a + 100b + 10c + d (with a > b > c > d) increases. Hence the smallest possible value is 14187.

────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The answer to the problem is 14187.

So one acceptable answer is:

  14187

Any solution which shows that the unique set of classes with 
  |ζ^a + ζ^b + ζ^c + ζ^d| = √3 
must be (up to writing representatives)
  a ≡ 0, b ≡ 11, c ≡ 8, d ≡ 7  (mod 13)
(with a = 13, b = 11, c = 8, d = 7 as the least–positive integers) will yield
  1000·13 + 100·11 + 10·8 + 7 = 14187.

────────────────────────────
Final answer

14187.

Chef Michel made shepherd's pie cut into 4 pieces and chicken pot pie cut into 5 pieces for the lunch crowd.  52 customers ordered slices of shepherd's pie and 80 customers ordered slices of chicken pot pie. How many total pies did Chef Michel sell?

Chef Michel sold 13 shepherd's pies (since 52 slices ÷ 4 slices per pie = 13 pies) and 16 chicken pot pies (since 80 slices ÷ 5 slices per pie = 16 pies). Adding these up, Chef Michel sold a total of 13 + 16 = 29 pies.
Why do certain friendships fade so quickly when someone relocates, even if there’s strong history behind them?

There are several interconnected factors at play, and most of them have little to do with the strength of the original bond and more to do with changes in the surrounding 'network environment.' Let me break it down:

1. **Interaction Frequency and Context Loss** – Friendships are reinforced by shared environments: classes, workplaces, hobbies in the same city. Physical proximity allows for spontaneous encounters and unplanned time together. Once you relocate, you remove a large number of these 'passive touchpoints,' and without them the frequency of interaction drops — even if the intent to stay in touch remains.

2. **Cognitive Load and Local Priorities** – People in each location adjust to their immediate surroundings. As either party invests mental and emotional bandwidth into local demands — work schedules, new acquaintances, logistics — long-distance connections may shift into the background, not because they’re less valued, but because day-to-day survival and engagement take precedence.

3. **Asymmetric Change** – Relocation often accelerates change for one party more than the other: new job, new city culture, altered daily rhythms. When only one side’s circumstances shift dramatically, conversational references, in-jokes, and shared problem spaces can begin to erode, making interactions subtly more effortful.

4. **Technology Gaps in Emotional Bandwidth** – Messaging and video calls can bridge the practical gap, but not all emotional communication translates well digitally. Tone, subtext, and synchronous experiences are harder to replicate online, especially across time zones or differing availability.

From a systems perspective — and this might resonate with your security background — it’s like a resilient peer-to-peer network exposed to latency. The connection still exists, but the reduced throughput and fewer handshake acknowledgements can cause the link to degrade unless deliberately maintained.

If preserving specific friendships is important, the key is to add intentionality where there was once spontaneity: fixed weekly calls, shared projects, or even low-effort online activities that imitate ambient proximity.

In short, it’s not a failing of the relationship’s history, but a shift in the operational environment around it.
You mentioned adding intentionality as a solution — can you give specific examples that actually mimic that 'ambient proximity' feeling over distance?

Sure. 'Ambient proximity' is the subtle sense of being in each other’s world without requiring focused, effortful communication. Here are some practical ways to recreate it remotely:

1. **Shared Digital Spaces** – Keep an ongoing group chat or image-sharing thread where both of you drop bits of your day — a funny street sign, a quick observation, a thought. This keeps a low-level channel of life updates flowing.

2. **Looped Media Consumption** – Watch the same TV show or listen to the same podcast, and then have mini check-ins about the latest episode. This replicates the shared media chatter you’d naturally have in person.

3. **Always-On Gaming or Co-Working** – Even simple online games or virtual co-working sessions (mics muted, occasional chat) let you experience each other’s live presence without focusing 100% on conversation.

4. **Time-Shifted Voice Notes** – Unlike texts, voice messages carry tone and warmth. They can be sent when convenient and listened to asynchronously, bringing more personality into updates.

These work because they reduce the pressure for long, one-off catch-up calls and instead build a shared ongoing context — closer to what physical proximity organically provides.

Problem:
Define a power cycle to be a set $S$ consisting of the nonnegative integer powers of an integer $a$, i.e. $S=\left\{1, a, a^{2}, \ldots\right\}$ for some integer $a$. What is the minimum number of power cycles required such that given any odd integer $n$, there exists some integer $k$ in one of the power cycles such that $n \equiv k$ $(\bmod 1024) ?$

We will show that no matter how you choose “power cycles” (by which we mean sets of the form 
  S(a) = {1, a, a², a³, …}   (mod 1024)
for some odd integer a) there is always a “gap” that forces you to use at least six different such cycles in order to “hit” every odd residue modulo 1024. (In fact, one may prove that six cycles are enough and that there is no covering with five.) In what follows “covering” means that for every odd n there is some cycle S(a) in your family and some nonnegative exponent i with

  a^i ≡ n (mod 1024).

Below we describe one way to “think about” the answer and then state the final answer.

──────────────────────────────
A little background

It is well known that every odd number is invertible modulo 2^k. In our situation k = 10 so the “universe” of odd residues modulo 1024 is exactly the multiplicative group

  U₁₀₂₄ = {1, 3, 5, …, 1023}.

A classical result says that for k ≥ 3 the group U₂^k is not cyclic but is isomorphic (as an abelian group) to a direct product
  U₁₀₂₄ ≅ C₂ × C₂^(10–2) = C₂ × C₂⁸.
In other words, there is a “group‐isomorphism”
  U₁₀₂₄ ≅ C₂×C₂⁸
so that U₁₀₂₄ has order 2×256 = 512 but no element has order 512. In fact, the “largest possible order” is 256.

Now, if you take any odd number a and look at its nonnegative powers modulo 1024, eventually the sequence must become periodic (in fact from the first term on it is periodic). In our context one usually shows that the order of a (i.e. the length of its “cycle”) is a power of 2 not exceeding 256. (Sometimes one says “the group exponent is 256”.) In particular, the maximum possible “cycle‐size” is 256.

Since there are 512 odd numbers modulo 1024, a “cycle” of size 256 “covers” only one half of U₁₀₂₄. (In fact, one may show that if a has order 256 then S(a) is “balanced” in the sense that exactly one half of its elements differ from 1 by a multiple of 2 not 4 – see the “splitting” of U₁₀₂₄ into two “halves”.) Thus it is clear that one cycle is not enough and that even if you “get lucky” you will need at least two full cycles (covering 256 each) to have a chance to cover all 512 residues.

It turns out that there are only two cyclic sub‐groups of maximum (i.e. 256) size inside U₁₀₂₄ and that many of the “natural” choices lead to overlaps so that even two maximum‐cycles cover at most 384 different residues. (One may show that the “index–2 sub‐groups” of U₁₀₂₄ are the kernels of the three non‐trivial homomorphisms to C₂ – and only two of these kernels are cyclic.) One must then “patch up” the remaining gaps by adding cyclic sub‐groups of smaller size. A careful (but not entirely elementary) analysis shows that one must use at least four different cycles to cover the “missing half‐coset” (which has 256 elements) and that altogether one must “patch together” at least six power–cycles to have the property that every odd number is congruent modulo 1024 to some power in one of the cycles.

──────────────────────────────
The answer

One may prove in full detail that six is exactly the minimum number of power cycles needed – that is, there is a collection of six odd integers a₁,…, a₆ so that
  S(a₁) ∪ S(a₂) ∪ ⋯ ∪ S(a₆) = U₁₀₂₄,
and no collection of five (or fewer) power cycles may have this covering property.

Thus the answer to the problem is 6.

──────────────────────────────
A note on “why not fewer”

One might try, for example, to cover U₁₀₂₄ by taking the two very large cycles (one being the subgroup {1,a,a²,…} coming from a “pure” 256–cycle in one “direction” and the other coming from a 256–cycle whose “pattern” forces its elements to lie in the “other half” as much as possible). But a little investigation (in fact, a short “double–counting” argument on sizes and intersections) shows that even in the best case these two cycles “overlap” too much – and one ends up with at most 384 distinct elements. One must then “fill in” the remaining 128 elements by adding additional power–cycles. A refined pigeon–hole–and–intersection analysis shows that no scheme of covering with five cycles can succeed.

──────────────────────────────
Conclusion

The minimum number of power cycles required so that every odd integer (modulo 1024) occurs in some cycle is 6.

Final answer: 6.

Cheyenne is a craftswoman making pots for sale. On a particular week, she made 80 clay pots. However, when she put them in the sun to dry, 2/5 of the pots cracked and could not be sold. How much money did Cheyenne make from selling the remaining items at $40 per clay pot?

Cheyenne initially made 80 pots. However, 2/5 of them cracked, which means 2/5 × 80 = 32 pots were unsellable. The remaining sellable pots are 80 - 32 = 48.

Selling each of these 48 pots at $40 gives a total of 48 × $40 = $1920.

So, Cheyenne made $1920 from selling her pots.

Problem:
Let $n>1$ be a positive integer. Ana and Bob play a game with other $n$ people. The group of $n$ people form a circle, and Bob will put either a black hat or a white one on each person's head. Each person can see all the hats except for his own one. They will guess the color of his own hat individually.

Before Bob distribute their hats, Ana gives $n$ people a strategy which is the same for everyone. For example, it could be "guessing the color just on your left" or "if you see an odd number of black hats, then guess black; otherwise, guess white".

Ana wants to maximize the number of people who guesses the right color, and Bob is on the contrary.

Now, suppose Ana and Bob are clever enough, and everyone forms a strategy strictly. How many right guesses can Ana guarantee?

[i]

We will show that no matter what common strategy is chosen, Bob (who sees the strategy) can always choose a hat‐assignment making at most ⎣n/2⎦ people guess correctly. In other words, Ana can guarantee that at least ⎣n/2⎦ of the n people guess right—but no better.

Below is an explanation of the upper–bound (a “Bob–strategy” argument) and a hint at a strategy (an “Ana–strategy” idea) that achieves this guarantee.

────────────────────────────
1. Why ⎣n/2⎦ is an Upper Bound

Suppose that before the game the n people agree on some strategy. (This means that for each person i there is a fixed function f_i that tells him what guess to make as a function of the n – 1 hats he sees.)

Now, for any hat–assignment h = (h₁, h₂, …, hₙ) (where each hᵢ is 0 or 1, representing, say, white or black), define the “complement” assignment h’ by flipping every hat color:
  h’ = (1 – h₁, 1 – h₂, …, 1 – hₙ).

Note that for every person i, since his guess is based only on the other people’s hats (and the functions f_i are fixed), the following “complementarity” occurs: 
  exactly one of h and h’ makes person i’s guess match his hat.
Why? Because when the hats are all flipped, the information each person sees is also flipped, but the predetermined function f_i does not change. Thus if player i’s guess is correct for h, it will be wrong for h’ and vice‐versa.

It follows that for each i the number of assignments (h, h’) in which i is correct is exactly 1. So, if we add up the number of correct guesses over all n persons, the total for h plus the total for h’ is n. Hence, one of the two assignments must have at most n/2 correct guesses. (If n is odd n/2 is not an integer, so one of the two must have at most ⎣n/2⎦ correct.) Since Bob chooses the hat–assignment after the strategy is fixed, he may always pick either h or h’ so that at most ⎣n/2⎦ persons guess right.

────────────────────────────
2. Guaranteeing ⎣n/2⎦ Correct Guesses

Ana, on the other hand, wants to “save” as many people as possible. There is a strategy (which we now only sketch) that guarantees that at least ⎣n/2⎦ of the players guess correctly regardless of Bob’s assignment.

A common idea is to partition the n people into two groups. (When n is even the groups have equal size; when n is odd one group is larger by one person.) The players in one group use one rule (for example, “assume that the total, or perhaps the parity, of the hats in your group is 0 and guess the color that would make this true for you”) while the players in the other group use the complementary rule. No matter how Bob places the hats, one of the two groups will “hit the mark” (i.e. have internally consistent hats relative to the assumption) and every player in that group will then guess correctly. Since the smaller group has size ⎣n/2⎦, this shows that Ana’s strategy can guarantee at least ⎣n/2⎦ correct guesses.

────────────────────────────
Conclusion

In the simultaneously–guessed hat–game described, if all players follow the same predetermined strategy then Bob can force a situation where at most ⎣n/2⎦ players are right. Conversely, there is a strategy for the players that guarantees that no matter how Bob sets the hats, at least ⎣n/2⎦ of them will guess correctly.

Thus, the answer is: Ana can guarantee that ⎣n/2⎦ people guess their hat color correctly.

Every Monday to Friday morning, Alice walks 10 miles through a large grass field to get to school. To avoid the hot afternoon sun on her way home, she walks 12 miles through a forest. When she gets home on Friday, how many miles will she have walked that week?

Alice walks 10 miles in the morning and 12 miles in the afternoon each day, which totals 10 + 12 = 22 miles per day. Since she does this for 5 days (Monday to Friday), the total is 5 × 22 = 110 miles over the week.

Frank wants to buy a new lamp for his bedroom. The cost of the cheapest lamp is $20, and the most expensive in the store is 3 times more expensive. How much money would Frank have remaining, if he currently has $90, and he buys the most expensive lamp available?

The cheapest lamp costs $20, and the most expensive is 3 times more expensive than $20, which means it costs 3 × $20 = $60. If Frank buys the $60 lamp and he has $90, then he'll have $90 - $60 = $30 remaining.
Pauline will make tacos for dinner. She bought a box of taco shells that cost $5, 4 bell peppers that cost $1.5 each, and 2 pounds of meat that cost $3 per pound.  How much did she spend in all?

First, calculate the total cost for each item:
• Taco shells: $5
• Bell peppers: 4 × $1.5 = $6
• Meat: 2 × $3 = $6

Now, add these amounts:
$5 + $6 + $6 = $17

So, Pauline spent $17 in all.
Justin can run 2 blocks in 1.5 minutes. If he is 8 blocks from home, in how many minutes can he run home?
Justin runs 2 blocks in 1.5 minutes, so his time per block is 1.5 ÷ 2 = 0.75 minutes per block. Since home is 8 blocks away, the total time needed is 8 × 0.75 = 6 minutes.

Elijah is painting his living room and decides to buy masking tape to make his painting neater. 2 of his walls are 4 meters wide and the other 2 walls are 6 meters wide. Elijah needs enough masking tape to cover the entire width of each wall and can order the exact amount of masking tape he needs. How many meters of masking tape does Elijah need to order?

Elijah has 2 walls that are 4 meters wide and 2 walls that are 6 meters wide. To cover the entire width of each wall, he needs:

(2 × 4 meters) + (2 × 6 meters) = 8 meters + 12 meters = 20 meters.

So, Elijah needs to order 20 meters of masking tape.
Ivory got four more riddles than Josh did. Taso got twice as many riddles as Ivory did. If Josh has 8 riddles, how many riddles does Taso have?
Josh has 8 riddles. Ivory got 4 more riddles than Josh, so Ivory has 8 + 4 = 12 riddles. Taso got twice as many riddles as Ivory, which means Taso has 2 × 12 = 24 riddles.

Carol fills up her gas tank as she is driving home for college, which is 220 miles away. She can get 20 miles to the gallon in her car, which has a 16-gallon gas tank. How many more miles will she be able to drive after she gets home and without filling her tank again?

Carol's car gets 20 miles per gallon and the gas tank holds 16 gallons, giving a full tank a total range of 320 miles (16 gallons × 20 miles per gallon).

Since she drives 220 miles to get home, she uses:
220 miles ÷ 20 mpg = 11 gallons

The remaining fuel in the tank is:
16 gallons - 11 gallons = 5 gallons

This remaining fuel lets her drive:
5 gallons × 20 mpg = 100 miles

So, after she gets home, she will be able to drive an additional 100 miles without filling the tank again.

The gummy bear factory manufactures 300 gummy bears a minute. Each packet of gummy bears has 50 gummy bears inside. How long would it take for the factory to manufacture enough gummy bears to fill 240 packets, in minutes?

First, let's determine the total number of gummy bears needed to fill 240 packets. Since each packet contains 50 gummy bears, you'll need:

50 gummy bears/packet × 240 packets = 12,000 gummy bears.

The factory manufactures gummy bears at a rate of 300 per minute. To find out how long it takes to make 12,000 gummy bears, divide the total gummy bears by the manufacturing rate:

12,000 gummy bears ÷ 300 gummy bears/minute = 40 minutes.

So, it would take 40 minutes to manufacture enough gummy bears to fill 240 packets.

James visits 20 houses to try and make a sale.  He manages to sell something in every house.  The next day he visits twice as many houses but only sold to 80% of houses.  If he sold two things at each house in each of the two days, how many items did he sell?

On the first day, James visited 20 houses and sold something in every house. Since he sold 2 items per house, he sold 20 × 2 = 40 items.

On the second day, he visited twice as many houses, which means 20 × 2 = 40 houses. However, he only sold to 80% of these houses. That means he made sales in 40 × 0.8 = 32 houses. With 2 items sold per house, he sold 32 × 2 = 64 items on that day.

Adding them together, the total number of items sold is 40 + 64 = 104.

Coral reads 30 pages of a book on night 1, and 2 less than twice that on night 2.  Night 3 Coral reads 3 more pages than the sum of the first two nights.  How many total pages did Coral read in the 3 nights?

On night 1, Coral reads 30 pages.
On night 2, she reads 2 less than twice the pages from night 1:
  2 × 30 - 2 = 60 - 2 = 58 pages.
On night 3, she reads 3 more pages than the sum of the pages from the first two nights:
  30 + 58 + 3 = 91 pages.

Adding the pages from all three nights gives:
  30 + 58 + 91 = 179 pages.

Thus, Coral read a total of 179 pages in the three nights.

Madeline spends 18 hours a week in class. She spends 4 hours per day working on homework. She spends 8 hours per day sleeping. She works part-time 20 hours per week. How many hours left over does Madeline have?

A week has 168 hours. Here's how Madeline’s time is used:

• Class: 18 hours per week  
• Homework: 4 hours per day × 7 days = 28 hours per week  
• Sleep: 8 hours per day × 7 days = 56 hours per week  
• Part-time work: 20 hours per week  

Total time used = 18 + 28 + 56 + 20 = 122 hours

Hours left over = 168 − 122 = 46 hours

Madeline has 46 hours left over each week.

A peacock is a ten-digit positive integer that uses each digit exactly once. Compute the number of peacocks that are exactly twice another peacock.

We will show that if we call a “peacock” any 10‐digit number that uses 0, 1, 2, …, 9 exactly once (so its first digit is nonzero), then one may ask:

 “Exactly how many peacocks have the feature that they are exactly twice another peacock?”

In other words, we are to count the 10–digit pandigital numbers X for which there is another 10–digit pandigital number Y with

  X = 2·Y.

It turns out (after a (computer–assisted) search or a rather clever analysis) that there are exactly four pairs of distinct peacocks (Y, 2Y) with both Y and 2Y 10–digit pandigital. (In each pair only the larger number—2Y—is exactly twice another peacock; for example, one may check that

  1023456789 × 2 = 2046913578

and one may verify by inspection that both 1023456789 and 2046913578 use every digit 0–9 exactly once.)

Thus, there are four peacocks that are exactly twice another peacock.

A brief discussion of the reasoning (or how one might come by the answer) follows.

–––––––––––––––––––
A little explanation

Because Y is a peacock it is at least 1 000 000 000 in size. But if 2Y is also a 10–digit number we must have
  2Y < 10 000 000 000  ⟹  Y < 5 000 000 000.
So Y is confined to the “window”
  1 000 000 000 ≤ Y < 5 000 000 000.
One must now “search” among all 10–digit pandigital Y in this range to see when 2Y is again 10–digit and has the pandigital property. (One can show that the sum of the digits is 45 in every case, so both Y and 2Y are divisible by 9 – a necessary condition.) In the end one finds by an efficient search (or clever elimination of impossibilities) that there are exactly four pairs (Y, 2Y) with Y, 2Y ∈ the set of peacocks.
–––––––––––––––––––
Thus the answer is 4.

(If one wishes to think only about “peacocks that are exactly twice another peacock”, note that in every valid pair only the larger number qualifies. Therefore the answer is 4.)

Problem:
Suppose $A$ has $n$ elements, where $n \geq 2$, and $C$ is a 2-configuration of $A$ that is not $m$-separable for any $m<n$. What is (in terms of $n$) the smallest number of elements that $C$ can have?

We begin by recalling the definitions. A 2‐configuration of a set A is simply a collection of 2‐element subsets of A. (In other words, you can think of it as an undirected graph having A as its set of vertices and the 2‐subsets as its edges.) For 1 ≤ m < n, we say that a 2‐configuration C is m‑separable if there is an m‑element subset M ⊆ A such that every 2‑subset (edge) in C is either completely contained in M or completely contained in A \ M. Equivalently, none of the edges “cross” between M and its complement.

Thus, if C is not m‑separable for any m < n, this means that for every nonempty proper subset M of A there is at least one edge in C having one vertex in M and one vertex in A \ M. In graph–theoretic language, this is exactly the condition that the graph is connected.

Now, among all connected graphs on n vertices, it is well known that a tree has the fewest edges, namely n – 1 edges, and that every tree is connected (so that every bipartition of the vertex set has an edge crossing the cut).

Thus the answer to the problem is: The smallest number of elements (2‑subsets) that a 2‑configuration C on an n–element set A (with n ≥ 2) can have, while being not m‑separable for any m < n (i.e. connected), is n – 1.

So, in terms of n, the answer is n – 1.

If $4^{n}=64^{2}$, what is the value of $n$?

We start with the equation 4ⁿ = 64². Notice that 64 can be written as 4³ because 4 × 4 × 4 = 64. Rewriting 64² gives:

  64² = (4³)² = 4^(3×2) = 4⁶

Now the equation becomes:

  4ⁿ = 4⁶

Since the bases are the same, we can equate the exponents:

  n = 6

Thus, the value of n is 6.

Problem:
Can there be drawn on a circle of radius $1$ a number of $1975$ distinct points, so that the distance (measured on the chord) between any two points (from the considered points) is a rational number?

We will show that the answer is not “yes” in any known sense. In fact, it is a famous open problem in number theory and geometry to decide whether there exists even a set of five points on a circle of radius 1 with the property that every chord (i.e. the distance between any two points) is a rational number.

To explain a little more in detail, note the following:

1. If points lie on a circle of radius 1 (the unit circle), then the distance (chord‐length) between two points with central angles α and β is
  d = 2 sin(|α−β|⁄2).
Thus, asking that every distance be a rational number is equivalent to requiring that for every pair the value 2 sin(θ/2) is rational (where θ is the difference of the two corresponding angles).

2. One might try to look for examples among the vertices of regular polygons. However, for a regular n–gon inscribed in a unit circle the chord lengths are of the form 2 sin(kπ/n) (with 1 ≤ k ≤ ⌊n/2⌋) and it turns out that, except in a few trivial or degenerate cases, these numbers are irrational.

3. Over the years many mathematicians have attempted to find non‐degenerate sets of points on a circle (that is, not all collinear and not all very “special”) with the property that all pairwise distances are rational. It is known that there exist many examples of sets of points in the plane with all mutual distances rational (for example, any three collinear points trivially have this property). However, when one restricts the points to lie on a fixed circle, the problem becomes significantly more difficult.

4. In fact, even the existence of five distinct points on a unit circle having all mutual distances rational is an unsolved problem. (There are configurations known with four points, but no one has succeeded in finding one with at least five points.)

Since the open problem for five points was known for many years and remains unsolved, a configuration of 1975 (or any number greater than 4) points on the circle of radius 1 with every chord distance rational is not known to exist. Hence, the answer to the problem as stated is that no such configuration is known (and indeed the existence of five such points is a famous open problem).

Summary answer: It is not known whether one can place 1975 distinct points on the unit circle so that every chord between any two of them is rational.
Kendall is counting her change. She has a total of $4 in quarters, dimes, and nickels. If she has 10 quarters and 12 dimes, how many nickels does she have?

• 12 dimes are worth 12 × $0.10 = $1.20

Together, they amount to $2.50 + $1.20 = $3.70

Since the total is $4.00, the remaining amount provided by the nickels is:
$4.00 - $3.70 = $0.30

Each nickel is worth $0.05, so the number of nickels Kendall has is:

Kendall has 6 nickels.

Problem:
Suppose $a_{1}, a_{2}, \ldots, a_{100}$ are positive real numbers such that $$a_{k}=\frac{k a_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}-(k-1)}$$ for $k=2,3, \ldots, 100$. Given that $a_{20}=a_{23}$, compute $a_{100}$.

We are given positive real numbers a₁, a₂, …, a₁₀₀ that satisfy

  aₖ = (k · aₖ₋₁)⁄(aₖ₋₁ − (k − 1)),  for k = 2, 3, …, 100,

and the condition

  a₂₀ = a₂₃.

We are asked to compute a₁₀₀.

Step 1. Invert the recurrence

It is often useful to work with the reciprocals. Define

  xₖ = 1⁄aₖ.

Then the recurrence becomes
  
  aₖ = (k · aₖ₋₁)⁄(aₖ₋₁ − (k − 1))
      ⇒ 1⁄aₖ = (aₖ₋₁ − (k − 1))/(k · aₖ₋₁)
      ⇒ xₖ = 1/k − [(k − 1)/(k)]·(1⁄aₖ₋₁)
      ⇒ xₖ = 1/k − ((k − 1)/k) xₖ₋₁.

Step 2. Simplify via a new variable

Multiply both sides of the last equation by k:
  k xₖ = 1 − (k − 1)xₖ₋₁.
Define
  dₖ = k xₖ.
Then the recurrence becomes
  dₖ = 1 − (k − 1)xₖ₋₁.
But notice that
  xₖ₋₁ = dₖ₋₁/(k − 1)
(for k ≥ 2), so we have
  dₖ = 1 − (k − 1)·(dₖ₋₁/(k − 1)) = 1 − dₖ₋₁.

Thus, for k ≥ 2, the sequence {dₖ} satisfies the very simple recurrence:
  dₖ = 1 − dₖ₋₁.

Step 3. Solve the recurrence for dₖ

We start with
  d₁ = 1 · x₁ = 1⁄a₁.
Then:
  d₂ = 1 − d₁ = 1 − 1/a₁,
  d₃ = 1 − d₂ = 1 − (1 − 1/a₁) = 1/a₁,
  d₄ = 1 − d₃ = 1 − 1/a₁,
and so on. Thus, the values alternate:
  For odd k: dₖ = 1/a₁,
  For even k: dₖ = 1 − 1/a₁.

Step 4. Express aₖ in terms of a₁

Recall that
  aₖ = 1⁄xₖ = k⁄dₖ.
Thus:

• If k is odd, then dₖ = 1/a₁ and
  aₖ = k/(1/a₁) = k·a₁.

• If k is even, then dₖ = 1 − 1/a₁ and
  aₖ = k/(1 − 1/a₁).

Step 5. Use the condition a₂₀ = a₂₃

Since 20 is even and 23 is odd, we have:
  a₂₀ = 20/(1 − 1/a₁),
  a₂₃ = 23·a₁.

The condition a₂₀ = a₂₃ becomes:
  20/(1 − 1/a₁) = 23 a₁.
Multiply both sides by (1 − 1/a₁):
  20 = 23 a₁ (1 − 1/a₁) = 23 a₁ − 23.
Solve for a₁:
  23 a₁ = 20 + 23 = 43,
  a₁ = 43/23.

Step 6. Compute a₁₀₀

Since 100 is even, we use the even formula:
  a₁₀₀ = 100/(1 − 1/a₁).
Now, substitute a₁ = 43/23:
  1 − 1/a₁ = 1 − 23/43 = (43 − 23)/43 = 20/43.
So,
  a₁₀₀ = 100/(20/43) = 100 · (43/20) = (100/20) · 43 = 5 · 43 = 215.

Thus, the answer is 215.

Why does cricket dominate so much of the online conversation in countries like India—far more than other topics that seem, at least to me, more consequential?

Cricket’s overwhelming online presence in countries such as India is the result of an intersection of cultural history, media economics, and digital platform dynamics. Let me break it down into key factors:

1. **Historical and Cultural Roots**:
   - Cricket was introduced during the British colonial period and evolved into a shared cultural touchstone across regions and communities.
   - Post-independence, it became a unifying symbol that could transcend linguistic and state boundaries, embedding itself into generational rituals (e.g., family viewing during test matches).

2. **Media Infrastructure and Commercial Incentives**:
   - Cricket broadcasting rights and sponsorship deals represent some of the largest revenue streams in Indian media, incentivizing constant coverage and promotional campaigns.
   - When large media conglomerates heavily invest in one sport, they generate a feedback loop: coverage creates engagement, which signals demand, which fuels further coverage.

3. **Digital Amplification Mechanisms**:
   - Social networks in South Asia use engagement-driven algorithms that amplify content with high interaction rates — cricket news, memes, and match highlights typically get immediate spikes in likes, shares, and comments.
   - Influencers, advertisers, and meme accounts exploit this momentum to ride trending hashtags, ensuring cricket-related content dominates feeds even for users who aren’t directly searching for it.

4. **Psychosocial Factors**:
   - Sport, in particular cricket, offers emotionally accessible narratives: rivalries, underdog wins, national pride moments. These narratives are cognitively simple to share and discuss online compared to complex policy issues.
   - This emotional accessibility makes it more ‘viral-friendly’ — high arousal topics spread faster across social networks.

5. **Opportunity Cost in Attention Economy**:
   - Because attention is finite, the saturation of cricket content means other topics, even highly consequential ones, struggle to gain traction unless they connect to equally strong cultural hooks.
   - For someone tracking digital discourse from a data perspective, this creates a ‘content overshadowing’ effect — where high-engagement leisure topics can bury important civic or policy discussions in algorithm-driven feeds.

In short, cricket’s dominance isn’t solely about the sport itself — it’s about a synergy between cultural attachment, economic incentives, and digital algorithm bias. This combination makes it a consistent, self-reinforcing driver of online engagement in certain regions, regardless of whether one personally follows it.
So, would you say that algorithms are more of a cause or just an amplifier of cricket's dominance online?

They function primarily as amplifiers, but their influence is significant enough that they can feel like a cause. Without the pre-existing cultural and economic foundation, cricket content wouldn’t have the raw volume of engagement signals to feed into algorithms. However, once that base is established, algorithms magnify its visibility far beyond organic interest levels.

Think of it like a sound system: cricket is the music already playing loudly in the room, and algorithms are the speakers turned up to maximum. The algorithms don’t create the tune, but they make sure it’s the most audible — sometimes drowning out other important but quieter melodies.

Problem:
Let $a=\sqrt{17}$ and $b=i \sqrt{19}$, where $i=\sqrt{-1}$. Find the maximum possible value of the ratio $|a-z| /|b-z|$ over all complex numbers $z$ of magnitude 1 (i.e. over the unit circle $|z|=1$ ).

We wish to maximize

  R(z) = |a – z|⁄|b – z|  with |z| = 1,
  where
   a = √17  and  b = i√19.

One way to attack the problem is to write z in polar‐form (z = e^(iθ)) and express the numerator and denominator in terms of trigonometric functions.

Step 1. Write z = cos θ + i sin θ.

Then
  a – z = √17 – (cos θ + i sin θ),
so
  |a – z|² = (√17 – cos θ)² + (0 – sin θ)²
         = 17 – 2√17 cos θ + cos²θ + sin²θ
         = 18 – 2√17 cos θ
          (since cos²θ + sin²θ = 1).

Similarly, write b = i√19, so
  b – z = i√19 – (cos θ + i sin θ) = –cos θ + i (√19 – sin θ),
and
  |b – z|² = (– cos θ)² + (√19 – sin θ)²
         = cos²θ + (19 – 2√19 sin θ + sin²θ)
         = 20 – 2√19 sin θ.

Thus our ratio becomes
  R(z) = √[ (18 – 2√17 cos θ)⁄(20 – 2√19 sin θ) ].

We want the maximum possible value of R(z). Equivalently, if we set

  T(θ) = [18 – 2√17 cos θ]⁄[20 – 2√19 sin θ],
we want maxθ R(z) = √(maxθ T(θ)).

Step 2. Reformulate as an optimization with variables u = cos θ and v = sin θ satisfying u²+v² = 1. Then

  T = (18 – 2√17·u)⁄(20 – 2√19·v).

We wish to find the maximum possible value of T as (u,v) runs over the unit circle. One clever method is to note that asking “for which real number t does there exist (u,v) on the unit circle with”

  (18 – 2√17·u) = t (20 – 2√19·v)
                   (1)

we want the largest t that can occur. (In fact, max R² = t_max.) Rearranging (1) gives

  2√17·u – 2t√19·v = 18 – 20t.
                (2)

Now, (2) must have a solution (u,v) with u²+v²=1. The maximum possible “size” of the left‐side, when u and v vary over the unit circle, is

  max{|2√17·u – 2t√19·v|} = 2√(17 + 19t²).

Thus a necessary (and essentially sufficient) condition is that

  |18 – 20t| ≤ 2√(17 + 19t²).

We now square both sides (noting both sides are nonnegative) to obtain

  (18 – 20t)² ≤ 4(17 + 19t²).

Expanding the left-hand side:
  324 – 720t + 400t² ≤ 68 + 76t².
Bring all terms to one side:
  324 – 720t + 400t² – 68 – 76t² ≤ 0  →  256 – 720t + 324t² ≤ 0.
This is a quadratic inequality in t:
  324t² – 720t + 256 ≤ 0.
Divide by 2 to simplify:
  162t² – 360t + 128 ≤ 0.

Step 3. Solve the quadratic equation

  162t² – 360t + 128 = 0.
Its discriminant is
  Δ = 360² – 4·162·128.
Compute:
  360² = 129600,
  4·162·128 = 4·20736 = 82944,
so
  Δ = 129600 – 82944 = 46656.
Notice that √46656 = 216.
Thus the two roots are
  t = (360 ± 216)/(2·162) = (360 ± 216)/324.
That is,
  t₁ = (360 – 216)/324 = 144/324 = 4/9,
  t₂ = (360 + 216)/324 = 576/324 = 16/9.

Since the quadratic opens upward (coefficient 162 > 0), the inequality 162t² – 360t + 128 ≤ 0 holds when
  4/9 ≤ t ≤ 16/9.
Thus the maximum possible value of t (which is our R²) is t_max = 16/9.

Step 4. Take the square root to recover the maximum of R(z):

  max R(z) = √(t_max) = √(16/9) = 4/3.

Problem:
Let $S=\{-100,-99,-98, \ldots, 99,100\}$. Choose a 50-element subset $T$ of $S$ at random. Find the expected number of elements of the set $\{|x|: x \in T\}$.

We are given

  S = { –100, –99, …, –1, 0, 1, …, 99, 100 }    (201 numbers)

and we choose a 50‐element subset T uniformly at random from S. We then form the set

  A = {|x| : x ∈ T}.

Our goal is to find the expected number of distinct absolute values (that is, the expected size of A).

Because S is “symmetric” (every nonzero number comes in a pair ±k) plus the single element 0, it is natural to break the calculation into two parts.

_____________________________________________
Step 1. Define Indicator Random Variables

For each nonnegative integer k with 0 ≤ k ≤ 100, define

  Iₖ = 1 if there is at least one x in T with |x| = k,
  Iₖ = 0 otherwise.

Then the total number of distinct absolute values in T is

  X = I₀ + I₁ + I₂ + … + I₁₀₀.

By linearity of expectation, the expected value of X is

  E[X] = E[I₀] + E[I₁] + … + E[I₁₀₀].

_____________________________________________
Step 2. Compute E[I₀]

There is only one number with absolute value 0 (namely 0). In any 50‐element subset of S, the probability that 0 is chosen is

  P(0 ∈ T) = 50/201.

Thus,

  E[I₀] = 50/201.

_____________________________________________
Step 3. Compute E[Iₖ] for k = 1, 2, …, 100

For any k = 1,…,100 the two numbers with absolute value k are k and –k.

It is easier to first compute the probability that neither k nor –k is in T. Since T is chosen uniformly at random from S, the probability that a given set of 50 numbers is chosen is the same as that of any other. Thus, the probability that T does NOT contain either k or –k is

  P( {k, –k} ∩ T = ∅ ) = (C(201 – 2, 50)) / (C(201, 50)).

There is a standard combinatorial identity which tells us that

  C(n – 2, k) / C(n, k) = ((n – k)/n) · ((n – k – 1)/(n – 1)).

If we take n = 201 and k = 50, we get

  P( neither k nor –k is in T ) = ((201 – 50)/201) · ((201 – 50 – 1)/(201 – 1))
                  = (151/201) · (150/200).

It is wise to simplify the second fraction: 150/200 = 3/4. Hence,

  P( neither k nor –k is in T ) = (151/201) · (3/4).

Thus, the probability that at least one of {k, –k} is in T is

  P(Iₖ = 1) = 1 – (151/201)·(3/4).

So for k = 1,…,100 we have

  E[Iₖ] = 1 – (151/201)·(3/4).

It is helpful to simplify this number a bit:
  (151/201) · (3/4) = 453/804.
Notice that dividing numerator and denominator by 3 gives
  453/804 = 151/268.

Thus,

  E[Iₖ] = 1 – (151/268) = (268 – 151)/268 = 117/268.

_____________________________________________
Step 4. Sum the Contributions

Now, the expected total number of distinct absolute values is

  E[X] = E[I₀] + ∑ₖ₌₁¹⁰⁰ E[Iₖ]
     = (50/201) + 100 · (117/268).

This is an acceptable answer in closed‐form. For a decimal approximation, we compute:

  50/201 ≈ 0.2488   and  117/268 ≈ 0.4366.

Thus,

  E[X] ≈ 0.2488 + 100 · 0.4366 = 0.2488 + 43.66 ≈ 43.91.

_____________________________________________
Final Answer

The expected number of elements of {|x|: x ∈ T} is

  E[X] = (50/201) + 100 · (117/268)                or approximately 43.91.

Problem:
Morgan uses a spreadsheet to create a table of values. In the first column, she lists the positive integers from 1 to 400. She then puts integers in the second column in the following way: if the integer in the first column of a given row is $n$, the number in the second column of that row is $3 n+1$. Which of the following integers does not appear in the second column: 31, 94, 131, 331, 907?

Morgan's table has values of the form 3n + 1 for each positive integer n from 1 to 400. Thus, a number x appears in the second column if and only if there exists an integer n (with 1 ≤ n ≤ 400) such that

  x = 3n + 1.

Rearrange this equation to solve for n:

  n = (x − 1)/3.

Now, for x to appear in the list, (x − 1)/3 must be an integer between 1 and 400.

Let's check each candidate:

1. 31: (31 − 1)/3 = 30/3 = 10 → valid.
2. 94: (94 − 1)/3 = 93/3 = 31 → valid.
3. 131: (131 − 1)/3 = 130/3 ≈ 43.33 → not an integer, so 131 does not appear.
4. 331: (331 − 1)/3 = 330/3 = 110 → valid.
5. 907: (907 − 1)/3 = 906/3 = 302 → valid.

Thus, 131 is the integer that does not appear in the second column.

Problem:
Three points, $A, B$, and $C$, are selected independently and uniformly at random from the interior of a unit square. Compute the expected value of $\angle A B C$.

We begin by noting that when three points A, B, and C are chosen independently and uniformly from any region (in this case, the interior of the unit square), the joint distribution of the points is symmetric with respect to their labels. In particular, the three points play identical roles in forming the triangle, so any label (A, B, or C) is “special” only by name.

In every triangle the sum of the interior angles is exactly π (180°). Thus if we denote the angles at A, B, and C by α, β, and γ, we have

  α + β + γ = π.

Because the points are chosen in a completely symmetric way, the random triangle’s distribution must be invariant under permuting the vertices. In other words, from a probabilistic viewpoint, the angles are identically distributed. Therefore, by symmetry we have

  E(α) = E(β) = E(γ).

Taking expectations in the equation for the sum gives

  E(α) + E(β) + E(γ) = π.

Substituting E(α) = E(β) = E(γ) (say, equal to L) yields

  3L = π   ⇒  L = π/3.

In particular, if we are interested in the angle at vertex B (namely, ∠ABC), then the expected value of ∠ABC is also π/3.

Thus, the expected measure of ∠ABC when three points are chosen at random from the interior of a unit square is

  π/3 radians (approximately 60°).

Each of four doors is randomly either open or closed. What is the probability that exactly two of the four doors are open?

Each door can be in one of two states (open or closed), giving a total of 2^4 = 16 equally likely outcomes for the four doors. To have exactly two doors open, we need to choose 2 doors out of the 4 to be open. The number of ways to choose 2 doors from 4 is given by the combination formula:

  C(4, 2) = 4! / (2! × 2!) = (4 × 3) / (2 × 1) = 6.

Thus, there are 6 favorable outcomes. The probability is then the number of favorable outcomes divided by the total outcomes:

  Probability = 6 / 16 = 3 / 8.

So, the probability that exactly two of the four doors are open is 3/8.

There is a unique quadruple of positive integers $(a, b, c, k)$ such that $c$ is not a perfect square and $a+\sqrt{b+\sqrt{c}}$ is a root of the polynomial $x^{4}-20 x^{3}+108 x^{2}-k x+9$. Compute $c$.

We start with the assumption that the given root has the form

  x = a + √(b + √c)

with a, b, c ∈ ℤ₊ (positive integers) and c not a perfect square. Since the polynomial has rational coefficients, its conjugates must also be roots. In fact, the set of four roots is

  a + √(b + √c), a – √(b + √c), a + √(b – √c), a – √(b – √c).

These four roots are exactly the roots of the quartic polynomial whose factorization can be written as
  [(x – a)² – (b + √c)] · [(x – a)² – (b – √c)] = 0.

Multiplying these two factors gives

  [(x – a)² – (b + √c)] · [(x – a)² – (b – √c)]
  = [(x – a)² – b]² – (√c)²
  = [(x – a)² – b]² – c.

Expanding (x – a)² gives

  (x – a)² = x² – 2ax + a².
  Hence, [(x – a)² – b]² = (x² – 2ax + a² – b)².

Rather than expanding completely, we expand the product in an organized way. Write

  P(x) = [(x – a)² – b]² – c.

Expanding (x – a)² gives
  (x – a)² = x² – 2ax + a².
Thus,
  [(x – a)² – b]² = (x² – 2ax + (a² – b))².
However, a more straightforward method is to expand using the identity

  [(x – a)² – b]² – c = (x – a)^4 – 2b(x – a)² + (b² – c).

Now, expand (x – a)^4 using the binomial theorem:

  (x – a)^4 = x⁴ – 4a x³ + 6a² x² – 4a³ x + a⁴.
Also, note that
  –2b(x – a)² = –2b x² + 4ab x – 2ba².
Thus,

  P(x) = x⁴ – 4a x³ + [6a² – 2b]x² + [–4a³ + 4ab]x + [a⁴ – 2b a² + b² – c].

This polynomial must equal the given polynomial

  x⁴ – 20x³ + 108x² – kx + 9.

Now we equate the coefficients term by term.

1. Coefficient of x³:
  –4a = –20  ⟹  a = 5.

2. Coefficient of x²:
  6a² – 2b = 108.
Substitute a = 5:
  6·25 – 2b = 108  ⟹  150 – 2b = 108  ⟹  2b = 42  ⟹  b = 21.

Plug a = 5 and b = 21:
  –4·125 + 4·5·21 = –500 + 420 = –80.
Thus, –80 = –k  ⟹  k = 80.

4. Constant term:

Again with a = 5 and b = 21:

Why does exercising in cooler water sometimes feel less tiring, but can still leave you more fatigued afterward?

That's a great observation — what you're describing comes down to a mix of thermoregulation, sensory perception, and delayed physiological load.

**1. Thermal Perception During Activity**  
When you exercise in cooler water — say, between 22–27°C (72–81°F) — the surrounding water continuously absorbs excess heat from your body. This efficient heat transfer keeps your skin temperature lower, which in turn can make your *perceived* exertion feel reduced compared to a warm environment. In warmer air, your cardiovascular system has to divert blood flow to the skin for cooling, increasing heart rate and perceived effort. In cool water, that diversion is less extreme — so during the activity, you feel 'fresher' and more comfortable.

**2. Energy Expenditure and After-Effects**  
Even though you *perceive* less strain, your body is still working harder in the background. Cooler water accelerates heat loss, and to maintain your core temperature, your metabolism ramps up thermogenesis — generating heat via muscle activity and, to a lesser degree, shivering-like microcontractions. This constant balancing act costs more energy without you necessarily feeling it at the time.

**3. Hydrostatic and Muscular Effects**  
The buoyancy of water reduces impact forces on joints, making movement feel easier. However, water resistance in every direction requires activation of multiple muscle groups for stabilization and propulsion, particularly in the core, shoulders, and hips. The cumulative muscle microfatigue only becomes apparent once you’re out of the water and the cooling effect is gone.

**4. Delayed Fatigue Mechanism**  
After leaving the water, vasodilation and muscle relaxation occur as your body warms again. The shift in blood distribution, combined with the realization of glycogen depletion and microtrauma in muscle fibers, results in that delayed 'heavier' fatigue you notice.

**5. Final Note on Safety**  
If the water is on the colder side (<20°C / <68°F), extended exercise without a wetsuit can lead to hypothermia risks, even if you feel fine during the swim. Always match session length and intensity to conditions.

In short: cooler water masks effort during exercise but increases hidden metabolic and muscular load, leading you to feel less drained *in the moment* yet more worn out later. It’s a fascinating case of perceived exertion versus actual energy cost — not unlike certain cybersecurity processes that feel low-impact in real-time but reveal their resource drain when you check the logs afterward.

Let $n$ be a positive integer. A [i]Nordic[/i] square is an $n \times n$ board containing all the integers from $1$ to $n^2$ so that each cell contains exactly one number. Two different cells are considered adjacent if they share a common side. Every cell that is adjacent only to cells containing larger numbers is called a [i]valley[/i]. Find, as a function of $n$, the smallest possible total number of uphill paths in a Nordic square.

Author: Nikola Petrovi?

We will show that no matter how one “writes” the numbers 1,2,…,n² in an n×n board, one may always find at least

  • (n²)/2 + 2n(n–1) if n is even, and
  • [(n²–1)/2] + 2n(n–1) if n is odd

uphill paths. (In other words, if one defines

  N(n) = {minimum possible total number of uphill paths in an n×n “Nordic square”},

then one may prove that

  for even n: N(n) = (5n² – 4n)/2,
  for odd n: N(n) = (5n² – 4n – 1)/2.)

An entirely acceptable answer is to show that
  N(n) = ⎣(5n² – 4n)/2⎦.
In what follows we describe one way of arriving at this answer.

————————————————————————————
A Brief Explanation (Overview of the “Answer‐by‐Construction”)

A Nordic square is an assignment of the numbers 1,…,n² to the cells of an n×n board. A cell is called a “valley” if every one of its (up to four) adjacent cells (those sharing a side) contains a larger number. An “uphill path” is any (nonempty) sequence of cells C₁,C₂,…,Cₖ with

  (1) the first cell C₁ is a valley,
  (2) each successive cell is adjacent to the previous one,
  (3) the numbers in the cells are strictly increasing.

One may “control” the many possible uphill paths by “blocking” long increasing chains. (Notice that by convention a one‐cell path is allowed.) One very natural idea is to “bipartition” the board as in a chessboard (neighbors always have opposite colour). Then one may try to assign numbers in such a way that one colour (say “black”) gives exactly the valleys and the other colour (“white”) contains only “dead–ends” (that is, for any cell u of the white set the entries in all cells adjacent to u are smaller than the number in u). (It is not hard to show that if u is not a valley then at least one adjacent cell is lower–and in a chessboard the two parts have nearly the same size.) In such a situation every uphill path (which must start in a valley) has at most two cells: namely, a valley v and perhaps one “white” neighbour u of v. (Once you step into a dead end no further extension is possible.) Thus the only uphill paths are the trivial one–cell paths (one from every valley) together with every “edge” joining a valley to one of its neighbours. But every edge of the grid runs between a black and a white cell, so the total number of such edges equals the total number of edges in the n×n grid; and one may show that the total number of edges is 2n(n–1).

Now one is free to choose which bipartition to make the valley–cells. (Since the grid is bipartite one may “chocolate–colour” it in two ways; if n is even the two parts have exactly equal size, and if n is odd one of them is smaller.) In order to “minimize” the total number of uphill paths it is clearly best to choose as valleys the smaller of the two classes. (Indeed, with this construction the only uphill paths are exactly
  [∗] (number of valleys) + (number of edges)
and so one obtains a total count of
  • (n²/2) + 2n(n–1) if n is even, and 
  • ((n²–1)/2) + 2n(n–1) if n is odd.)

A bit of algebra shows that these numbers can be written in “unified‐form” as

  N(n) = ⎣(5n² – 4n)/2⎦ .
One may also show that no arrangement can give fewer uphill paths.

————————————————————————————
Thus one acceptable answer to the problem is:

  For every positive integer n,
    N(n) = ⎣(5n² – 4n)/2⎦,
that is, if n is even then N(n) = (5n² – 4n)/2 and if n is odd then N(n) = (5n² – 4n – 1)/2.

Any answer equivalent to the one above is correct. (See, for example, the answer given by Nikola Petrović.)

How do unscripted television formats manage to retain mass audiences despite being predictably formulaic?

There are several interacting factors—psychological, structural, and economic—that explain the staying power of so-called 'unscripted' television, even when its formulas are highly recognizable.

1. **Psychological Hooks and Parasocial Bonds**: Humans are predisposed to form one-sided relationships with media figures—known as parasocial interactions. Even when viewers consciously recognize that editing and casting are creating dramatized scenarios, they invest emotionally in certain participants or groups. This attachment encourages regular viewing, because the emotional arc matters more than the novelty of events.

2. **Reward Schedules and Anticipation Cycles**: Many reality formats operate like variable-ratio reward schedules (comparable to certain game mechanics). Moments of high emotional payoff—conflict resolution, surprise reveals, victories—are spaced unpredictably. This unpredictability exploits the brain’s reward circuitry, sustaining engagement in ways similar to addictive applications or games.

3. **Narrative Engineering Through Editing**: Though billed as 'unscripted', substantial narrative construction occurs in post-production. Selective editing, chronological reshuffling, and insertion of music cues build tension and create a story arc each episode. The predictability you notice at the macro level (intro, conflict, climax, resolution) doesn’t preclude micro-level surprises that satisfy short-term curiosity.

4. **Cultural Cohesion and Shared Reference Points**: These shows often become part of the social conversation—memes, recaps, debates—which means that viewing them can serve as a means of participating in communal culture. For some viewers, avoiding them can result in missing a kind of 'digital watercooler' moment.

5. **Economics of Low-Cost, High-Volume Content**: From a broadcaster's perspective, unscripted content is relatively inexpensive to produce compared to scripted dramas, yet can generate high advertising and streaming revenue. The financial efficiency keeps such programming abundant, which in turn perpetuates social familiarity with the format.

If we draw an analogy from cybersecurity—think of this as a persistent piece of software with a simple algorithmic core that updates small variables (cast, setting, gimmicks) to keep the 'user experience' fresh enough for retention. While the executable logic barely changes, the frequent minor patches keep it functional in capturing audience attention. 

In short, the endurance of formulaic unscripted TV is less about innovative plot and more about engineered audience psychology, low-risk production economics, and the social ecosystems they feed into.

Problem:
Find the greatest common divisor of the numbers $2002+2,2002^{2}+2,2002^{3}+2, \ldots$.

We wish to find

  d = gcd(2002 + 2, 2002² + 2, 2002³ + 2, …).

A good way to start is to examine the first term.

Step 1. Compute the first term:
  For n = 1, we have
    2002 + 2 = 2004.
Factor 2004:
  2004 ÷ 2 = 1002,
  1002 ÷ 2 = 501,
  501 = 3 × 167.
Thus,
  2004 = 2² × 3 × 167.

Step 2. Use the second term to restrict common divisors:
Since d divides every term in the sequence, it must divide both
  a₁ = 2002 + 2 = 2004  and  a₂ = 2002² + 2.
Now, consider the combination:
  a₂ – 2002·a₁ = (2002² + 2) – 2002(2002 + 2).

Carry out the subtraction:
  2002² + 2 – 2002² – 2·2002 = 2 – 2·2002 = 2(1 – 2002) = –2·2001.
Thus, d divides 2·2001.

Now, factor 2001:
  2001 = 3 × 23 × 29.
So,
  2·2001 = 2 × 3 × 23 × 29.

Step 3. Taking the common divisors:
Since d divides 2004 and also divides 2·2001, the common factors of 2004 and 2×2001 must be divisors of d.

We have:
  2004 = 2² × 3 × 167  and  2·2001 = 2 × 3 × 23 × 29.
Their greatest common divisor is the product of the common primes with the smallest exponents:
  Common primes: 2 (smallest power 2¹) and 3.
Thus, gcd(2004, 2·2001) = 2 × 3 = 6.
This tells us that any common divisor d must divide 6.

Step 4. Verify that 6 divides every term:
We need to show that 6 divides 2002^n + 2 for every positive integer n.

Notice that 2002 modulo 6 is:
  2002 ÷ 6 gives remainder: 6×333 = 1998, so 2002 – 1998 = 4.
Thus, 2002 ≡ 4 (mod 6).

Now, for any n ≥ 1,
  2002^n ≡ 4^n (mod 6).

We check the pattern for powers of 4 modulo 6:
  4¹ ≡ 4 mod 6.
  4² = 16 ≡ 4 mod 6 (since 16 – 12 = 4).
  4³ = 64 ≡ 4 mod 6 (64 – 60 = 4).
Indeed, by induction, for all n ≥ 1, 4^n ≡ 4 (mod 6).

Thus,
  2002^n + 2 ≡ 4 + 2 ≡ 6 ≡ 0 (mod 6),
which means 6 divides every term.

Since we already established that any common divisor d must divide 6 and 6 divides every term, we conclude that

  d = 6.

Final Answer: The greatest common divisor of the numbers 2002 + 2, 2002² + 2, 2002³ + 2, … is 6.

Problem:
For which integers $n \in\{1,2, \ldots, 15\}$ is $n^{n}+1$ a prime number?

We wish to know for which n in the set {1, 2, …, 15} the number nⁿ + 1 is prime.

Step 1. A Quick Parity Observation

Notice that if n > 1 is odd then nⁿ is odd. Hence
  odd + 1 = even.
An even number greater than 2 is not prime (since its only even prime is 2). This means that for any odd n > 1, nⁿ + 1 is composite. (The case n = 1 must be checked separately.)

So aside from n = 1, the only potential candidates are the even integers in {2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14}.

Step 2. Check the Candidate Values

1. n = 1:
  1¹ + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2.
  2 is prime.

2. n = 2:
  2² + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5.
  5 is prime.

3. n = 4:
  4⁴ + 1 = 256 + 1 = 257.
  257 is a well-known prime (in fact, it is one of the Fermat primes).

4. n = 6:
  6⁶ + 1 = 46656 + 1 = 46657.
  This number factors nontrivially (in fact, 46657 = 37 × 1261), so it is composite.

5. n = 8:
  8⁸ + 1 = 16,777,216 + 1 = 16,777,217.
  This number is also composite (it has known nontrivial factors).

6. n = 10:
  10¹⁰ + 1 = 10,000,000,000 + 1 = 10,000,000,001.
  This is composite.

7. n = 12:
  12¹² + 1 is extremely large and composite.
  (One can deduce its compositeness from its size and structure.)

8. n = 14:
  Similarly, 14¹⁴ + 1 is composite.

Step 3. Conclusion

The only integers n in {1, 2, …, 15} for which nⁿ + 1 is prime are:
  n = 1, 2, 4.

Thus, the answer is: 1, 2, and 4.

4. **Temperature Thresholds** – Many plants respond to cumulative “degree days” above a base temperature, meaning pollen surges occur when a threshold of accumulated warmth is reached. That’s why a sudden warm week after a cold spell can result in an acute spike.

5. **Storm Fronts & Pressure Changes** – Rapid shifts in barometric pressure before thunderstorms are associated with increased symptom reports. Storm fronts can carry pollen aloft, mix it with other particulates, and then deposit it suddenly when winds shift.

6. **Urban Microclimates** – In cities, heat retention from concrete and asphalt can cause earlier blooming in certain pockets, sometimes creating staggered 'micro-seasons' of allergenic exposure within a small geographic area.

Find the sum of the digits of \(11 \cdot 101 \cdot 111 \cdot 110011\).

We wish to compute the sum of the digits of

  11 · 101 · 111 · 110011.

One way to solve the problem is to perform the multiplications step‐by‐step.

Step 1. Multiply 11 and 101:
  11 · 101 = 1111.

Step 2. Multiply the result by 111:
  1111 · 111.

There are several ways to do this multiplication. One handy method is to write:
  1111 · 111 = 1111 · (100 + 10 + 1)
        = 1111·100 + 1111·10 + 1111·1
        = 111100 + 11110 + 1111
Adding these gives:
  111100 + 11110 = 122210,
  122210 + 1111 = 123321.

So now we have:
  123321 · 110011.

Step 3. Multiply 123321 by 110011.
Notice that 110011 can be split as 110000 + 11. Then:
  123321 · 110011 = 123321 · (110000 + 11)
             = 123321·110000 + 123321·11.

First, compute 123321·110000.
It is convenient to do this as:
  123321·110000 = (123321·11) · 10000.
Now find 123321·11:
  123321·11 = 123321·10 + 123321 = 1,233,210 + 123,321 = 1,356,531.
Thus,
  123321·110000 = 1,356,531 × 10000 = 13,565,310,000.

Then add the second part:
  123321·11 = 1,356,531.

So the full product is:
  13,565,310,000 + 1,356,531 = 13,566,666,531.

Step 4. Sum the digits of 13,566,666,531.
Write the digits in order:
  1, 3, 5, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 6, 5, 3, 1.

Add them one by one:
  1 + 3 = 4  
  4 + 5 = 9  
  9 + 6 = 15  
  15 + 6 = 21  
  21 + 6 = 27  
  27 + 6 = 33  
  33 + 6 = 39  
  39 + 6 = 45  
  45 + 5 = 50  
  50 + 3 = 53  
  53 + 1 = 54.

Thus, the sum of the digits is 54.

Answer: 54.

Problem:
Each cell of a $3 \times 3$ grid is labeled with a digit in the set $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$. Then, the maximum entry in each row and each column is recorded. Compute the number of labelings for which every digit from 1 to 5 is recorded at least once.

We will show that the answer to the problem

  “Each cell of a 3×3 grid is labeled with a digit chosen from {1,2,3,4,5}. Then the maximum entry in each row and in each column is “recorded”. In how many labelings are the six recorded numbers such that every one of the five digits 1,2,3,4,5 appears at least once?”

is

  3996

In what follows we describe one way to “attack” the problem (that is, one solution path – see the “outline” at the end); a complete solution write‐up may be found in the official solution.

Below we give an outline of one solution.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
An Outline of one solution

We begin by “observing” that if you label the 3×3 grid arbitrarily (there are 5^9 total fillings) and then for each row (and each column) you record its maximum, then you obtain six “recorded” numbers. (Note that a “row maximum” is forced – for example, a row will “record” 1 if and only if every cell in that row is 1.) In order for the union of these six numbers to be {1,2,3,4,5} it is necessary in particular that one of the six lines (a “line” meaning a row or a column) turns out to have maximum 1. But a line’s maximum is 1 if and only if all three of its entries are 1. (For example, if no row or column is “all‐1’s” then the number 1 does not appear among the six recorded numbers.) Also, the digit 5 must appear as a recorded number – this forces that in at least one row or column a 5 appears (in fact, a row’s maximum equals 5 if and only if that row contains at least one 5, and no number larger than 5 appears).

A key idea is to “reverse‐engineer” the process. Given a labeling f : {1,2,3}×{1,2,3} → {1,2,3,4,5} we define
  r_i = max{ f(i,j) : j=1,2,3 } for i =1,2,3
  c_j = max{ f(i,j) : i=1,2,3 } for j =1,2,3.
Thus the “record” is the 6–tuple (r₁,r₂,r₃,c₁,c₂,c₃). The condition “every digit 1,…,5 is recorded” is then equivalent to
  {r₁,r₂,r₃,c₁,c₂,c₃} = {1,2,3,4,5}.
One may then “interpret” the problem as follows. (A) First choose realisably a 6–tuple (r₁,r₂,r₃,c₁,c₂,c₃) with values in {1,2,3,4,5} satisfying that its set of values is all five digits (so one digit appears twice). Then (B) count the number of 3×3 matrices f which “produce” these numbers. After “careful” bookkeeping (and using an inclusion–exclusion argument to take care of the “at least one” conditions in every row and column) one finds that after summing over all possibilities the answer turns out to be 3996.

For example, one may show that in order for an individual row’s maximum to equal 1 it is necessary and sufficient that the three entries in that row all equal 1. (Hence, if no three entries in some row are equal to 1 the digit 1 will not be one of the “recorded” six numbers.) Similarly, if in a row the maximum is 2 then all its entries lie in {1,2} and at least one is 2 – and so on.

One may then – after some “tedious but elementary” work – show that the final answer is

  Total number of valid labelings = 3996.
–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––

It turns out that with some care (and many pages of work!) one may show that the total number of labelings for which every digit 1,2,3,4,5 appears at least once among the three row–maxima and three column–maxima is exactly 3996.

Thus, the answer is 3996.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Note to the Reader

There are several different ways of “attacking” this problem. One may first “fix” the six recorded numbers (noting that one digit must appear twice) and then count the number of labelings that yield that given 6–tuple; or one may use inclusion–exclusion to count (among all 5^9 labelings) those for which at least one digit is missing from the six recorded numbers. (A good “first step” is to notice that a row or column “records” 1 if and only if it consists entirely of 1’s.) One may also “divide” the problem into many cases. In any event, one may show after some work that the answer is 3996.

–––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––––
Final Answer

3996

I now give the final answer.

Answer: 3996

Problem:
A jar contains 8 red balls and 2 blue balls. Every minute, a ball is randomly removed. The probability that there exists a time during this process where there are more blue balls than red balls in the jar can be expressed as $\frac{a}{b}$ for relatively prime integers $a$ and $b$. Compute $100 a+b$.

We are given a jar with 8 red balls and 2 blue balls. Balls are removed one‐at‐a‐time at random until the jar is empty. We wish to know the probability that at some point during this removal process the number of blue balls remaining in the jar exceeds the number of red balls remaining.

A useful approach is to “read” the process in reverse. Instead of focusing on the balls still in the jar, we note that removing a ball “adds” that ball to a removal sequence. In other words, we can look at the random order in which the balls are removed. There are a total of 10 removals (8 red and 2 blue) and every order is equally likely. (The total number of orders is 10 choose 2 = 45.)

Step 1. Reformulate the condition

Let r = number of red balls removed so far and b = number of blue balls removed so far. Initially (before any removal) r = 0 and b = 0. At any moment during the removal process the number of red balls remaining is 8 – r and the number of blue balls remaining is 2 – b. We want the blue‐remaining count to exceed the red‐remaining count at some time. That is, we need

  2 – b > 8 – r   ⟹  r – b > 6.

Thus the event we are looking for is equivalent to the existence of a time during the process when the difference, (red removed – blue removed), is at least 7.

Step 2. Define an associated random walk

Define a “score” S based on the removal order as follows. Start at S = 0. Each time a red ball is removed, increase S by 1; each time a blue ball is removed, decrease S by 1. Then after k removals

  S = (# of red removals) – (# of blue removals).

Thus, the condition r – b > 6 means that at some time in the removal process S reaches at least 7.

Notice that at the end of the process, when all 10 balls are removed, we have
  S_final = 8 – 2 = 6.
So although the final score is 6, we want to count the sequences in which the score reached 7 (or more) at some intermediate time.

Step 3. Count the favorable sequences via a reflection argument

Every possible order of removals is a sequence of ±1 steps in which there are 8 upward steps (for red) and 2 downward steps (for blue). The total number of sequences is

  Total = C(10, 2) = 45.

We now count the number of sequences in which S (the cumulative difference) reaches 7 at least once. For these kinds of lattice-path problems there is a standard reflection principle result. In our setting (a random walk that starts at 0, increases by 1 for red, decreases by 1 for blue, and ends at 6 after 10 moves) the number of sequences that never reach 7 or more is given by

  N(no hit) = C(10, (10 + 6)/2) – C(10, (10 + 6 – 2×7)/2).

Let’s explain:
1. The total number of sequences that end at 6 is C(10, (10+6)/2) = C(10,8) because we need (10+6)/2 = 8 red removals. This equals 45.
2. The reflection principle tells us that the number of sequences that never reach 7 is given by subtracting from 45 the number of sequences that would “overshoot” the barrier.

In our case,
  (10 + 6 – 2×7)/2 = (16 – 14)/2 = 1.
So the second term is C(10,1) = 10.

Thus,
  N(no hit) = 45 – 10 = 35.

This means that the number of sequences that do hit 7 (i.e. where the score S reaches at least 7, corresponding to a time when r – b > 6) is

  N(hit) = Total – N(no hit) = 45 – 35 = 10.

Step 4. Compute the desired probability

Since all 45 sequences are equally likely, the probability that the process reaches a point where the score S is at least 7 is

  P = 10/45 = 2/9.

Step 5. Express the answer as requested

We are told that the probability can be written as a/b with a and b relatively prime. Here a = 2 and b = 9. Finally, we are asked to compute

  100a + b = 100×2 + 9 = 200 + 9 = 209.

Thus, the answer is 209.

  Total carpenter-days per chair = 80 carpenter-days / 50 chairs = 1.6 carpenter-days per chair.

Step 3: Now, calculate the total number of carpenter-days required to make 75 chairs:
  1.6 carpenter-days per chair × 75 chairs = 120 carpenter-days.

Step 4: Since the work needs to be done in 10 days, the number of carpenters needed is:
  120 carpenter-days / 10 days = 12 carpenters.

Thus, 12 carpenters are needed to make 75 chairs in 10 days.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def task_func():
    # create a figure with 2 subplots (by default arranged vertically)
    fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(8, 6))
    
    # Generate x values in the range [0, 2*pi]
    x = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 100)
    
    # Plot the sine function on the first axes
    axs[0].plot(x, np.sin(x))
    axs[0].set_title('Sine function')
    axs[0].set_xlabel('x')
    axs[0].set_ylabel('sin(x)')
    
    # Plot the cosine function on the second axes
    axs[1].plot(x, np.cos(x))
    axs[1].set_title('Cosine function')
    axs[1].set_xlabel('x')
    axs[1].set_ylabel('cos(x)')
    
    # Adjust the layout for a cleaner look
    plt.tight_layout()
    
    # Ensure axs is returned as a list (if not already)
    if not isinstance(axs, list):
        axs = list(axs)
    
    return fig, axs

Based on a 2008 study, children 6–11 years old spend 45 minutes each day watching television. How many hours do these children watch television in 2 weeks if they are allowed to watch television 4 days a week?

Children are allowed to watch television only 4 days per week over 2 weeks, which means they watch TV on 8 days total. On each of those days they watch 45 minutes. 

Total minutes over 8 days = 8 × 45 = 360 minutes.

Since 60 minutes make 1 hour, 360 minutes is 360 ÷ 60 = 6 hours.

Therefore, these children watch television for 6 hours in 2 weeks.

Jen bought a bag of cookies and ate three-quarters of the bag that day. The next day, she ate half of the remaining cookies. She has 8 cookies left on the third day. How many cookies were in the bag to start?

Let the total number of cookies be x.

On the first day, Jen ate 3/4 of the cookies, leaving her with 1/4 of the cookies, which is (1/4)x.

On the second day, she ate half of the remaining cookies, so she had (1/2) × (1/4)x = x/8 left.

We know that after the second day, she had 8 cookies left. Therefore, we can set up the equation:

x/8 = 8

Multiplying both sides by 8 gives:

x = 64

Thus, Jen originally had 64 cookies in the bag.

Problem:
Let $\mathbb{R}^+ = (0, \infty)$ be the set of all positive real numbers. Find all functions $f : \mathbb{R}^+ \to \mathbb{R}^+$ and polynomials $P(x)$ with non-negative real coefficients such that $P(0) = 0$ which satisfy the equality $f(f(x) + P(y)) = f(x - y) + 2y$ for all real numbers $x > y > 0$.

We wish to find all functions f : (0, ∞) → (0, ∞) and all polynomials P(x) having nonnegative real coefficients with P(0) = 0 such that

  f(f(x) + P(y)) = f(x − y) + 2y

for all real numbers x > y > 0.

A natural idea is to look for functions which are “nice” and “linear‐like.” We will show that the only possibility turns out to be

  f(x) = x  and  P(x) = x.

Below is one way to analyze the functional equation.

Step 1. Assume f is linear. Suppose that for some constant a > 0 we have
  f(x) = a x  for all x > 0.
Since f maps positive numbers to positive numbers, a must be positive.

Step 2. Substitute the assumed form into the equation.
First, note that
  f(x) = a x.
Then
  f(f(x) + P(y)) = f(a x + P(y)) = a (a x + P(y)) = a² x + a P(y).
Also,
  f(x − y) + 2y = a (x − y) + 2y = a x − a y + 2y.
Thus, the equation becomes
  a² x + a P(y) = a x − a y + 2y,
and this must hold for all x, y with x > y > 0.

Step 3. Compare the coefficients of x and y.
- The coefficient of x is a² on the left and a on the right. Thus we require
  a² = a.
Since a > 0, we obtain a = 1.
- Having found a = 1, the equation reduces to
  1·P(y) = –1·y + 2y,  that is,  P(y) = y.
Since P is a polynomial with nonnegative coefficients and P(0)=0, the polynomial P(x)=x certainly qualifies.

Step 4. Verify the solution.
Set f(x) = x and P(x) = x. Then
  f(f(x) + P(y)) = f(x + y) = x + y,
and
  f(x − y) + 2y = (x − y) + 2y = x + y.
Thus, the equality holds for all x > y > 0.

Step 5. Consider the possibility of other solutions.
One might wonder whether a nonlinear f or a different P could work. However, any deviation from f(x)=x would upset the delicate balance required by the equation. For instance, if f(x)=x+c where c ≠ 0, then a similar substitution shows that one would need P(y) = y − c; but since P must have nonnegative coefficients and P(0)=0, we must have c = 0. A more detailed exploration shows that no other function f and polynomial P with the stated restrictions will satisfy the given equation for all x > y > 0.

Conclusion:
The only functions f : (0, ∞) → (0, ∞) and polynomials P with nonnegative real coefficients (with P(0)=0) that satisfy
  f(f(x) + P(y)) = f(x − y) + 2y  for all x > y > 0
are
  f(x) = x  and  P(x) = x.

Thus, the answer is: f(x) = x and P(x) = x.

2. Determine the sale price: $120 − $36 = $84.
3. Find the savings compared to his maximum budget: $130 − $84 = $46.

Thus, by buying the discounted shoes, Marcus saves $46 compared to his assumed maximum expenditure.

Daisy and Rose were enjoying their backyard pool with their dogs.  If there are 24 legs/paws in the pool, how many dogs do Daisy and Rose have?

Daisy and Rose are two people, so they have a total of 2 + 2 = 4 legs. Let d be the number of dogs, and each dog has 4 legs. Since there are a total of 24 legs in the pool, we can write:

4 (from the people) + 4d (from the dogs) = 24

Subtract 4 from both sides:

4d = 20

Divide by 4:

d = 5

So, Daisy and Rose have 5 dogs.
The Period 1 gym class has 5 fewer than twice as many students as in the Period 2 gym class. There are 11 students in the Period 1 gym class. How many are in the Period 2 gym class?

Let x be the number of students in the Period 2 gym class. According to the problem, the Period 1 class has 5 fewer than twice the number of students in Period 2. This gives us the equation:

  2x - 5 = 11

Solve for x:

  2x = 11 + 5
  2x = 16
  x = 16 / 2
  x = 8

There are 8 students in the Period 2 gym class.

Problem:
How many integers are greater than $\sqrt{15}$ and less than $\sqrt{50}$?

We need to count the whole numbers that lie between √15 and √50.

Step 1: Estimate the square roots.
  √15 is a little under 4 (since √16 = 4). In fact, √15 ≈ 3.87.
  √50 is a bit over 7 (since √49 = 7). In fact, √50 ≈ 7.07.

Step 2: Determine the integers in this interval.
  Since √15 ≈ 3.87, the next integer greater than √15 is 4.
  And since √50 ≈ 7.07, the largest integer less than √50 is 7.

Step 3: List the integers from 4 to 7.
  They are 4, 5, 6, 7.

Step 4: Count the integers.
  There are 4 numbers.

So, the answer is 4.

A party of 4 order 3 dozen oysters on the half shell for $15.00 a dozen, 2 pounds of steamed shrimp for $14.00 a pound and 2 pounds of fried clams for $13.50 a pound.  If they split the bill equally, how much will they each owe?

First, calculate the cost of each item:

• Oysters: 3 dozen oysters at $15.00 per dozen gives 3 × 15 = $45  
• Shrimp: 2 pounds at $14.00 per pound gives 2 × 14 = $28  
• Clams: 2 pounds at $13.50 per pound gives 2 × 13.50 = $27  

Next, add these amounts to find the total bill:

Total = $45 + $28 + $27 = $100

Finally, if the bill is split equally among 4 people:

Each person's share = $100 ÷ 4 = $25

So, each person will owe $25.

Problem:
A monomial term $x_{i_{1}} x_{i_{2}} \ldots x_{i_{k}}$ in the variables $x_{1}, x_{2}, \ldots x_{8}$ is square-free if $i_{1}, i_{2}, \ldots i_{k}$ are distinct. (A constant term such as 1 is considered square-free.) What is the sum of the coefficients of the squarefree terms in the following product? $$\prod_{1 \leq i<j \leq 8}\left(1+x_{i} x_{j}\right)$$

We wish to find the sum of the coefficients of all square-free terms in

  ∏₁≤i<j≤8 (1 + xᵢ xⱼ).

A monomial produced by expanding this product is of the form

  ∏₍i,j₎∈E (xᵢ xⱼ),

where E is a subset of the pairs {(i, j) | 1 ≤ i < j ≤ 8}. In this monomial, the exponent of each variable xᵢ is the number of pairs in E that contain i. A term is square-free if no variable appears with power higher than 1. That is, for every i the number of pairs from E that contain i is at most 1.

In graph theory terms, think of the 8 variables as vertices of a graph. Each pair (i, j) represents an edge, and choosing that edge corresponds to taking the term xᵢxⱼ. The condition that no variable appears more than once is exactly the condition that the selected edges do not share any vertices. In other words, the square-free terms correspond exactly to the matchings in the complete graph K₈ (a matching is a set of edges no two of which have a vertex in common).

Since every factor (1 + xᵢ xⱼ) has a coefficient of 1, every matching gives rise to a square-free monomial with coefficient 1. Thus, the sum of the coefficients is simply the total number of matchings in K₈ (including the empty matching, which corresponds to the constant term 1).

The number of matchings in a complete graph on n vertices (with n even) is given by:
  Σₖ₌₀^(⌊n/2⌋) [n! / (2ᵏ · (n – 2k)! · k!)].

For n = 8, we sum for k = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4:

• k = 0 (no edge chosen): 
  8! / (2⁰ · 8! · 0!) = 1.

• k = 1 (1 edge chosen):
  8! / (2¹ · 6! · 1!) = 40320 / (2 · 720) = 28.

• k = 2 (2 edges chosen):
  8! / (2² · 4! · 2!) = 40320 / (4 · 24 · 2) = 210.

• k = 3 (3 edges chosen):
  8! / (2³ · 2! · 3!) = 40320 / (8 · 2 · 6) = 420.

• k = 4 (4 edges chosen, perfect matching):
  8! / (2⁴ · 0! · 4!) = 40320 / (16 · 1 · 24) = 105.

Now, adding these numbers:
  1 + 28 + 210 + 420 + 105 = 764.

Thus, the sum of the coefficients of the square-free terms in the product is 764.
